newsitem.title: ITALY: Railway boss apologises for Italian train chaos.
newsitem.headline: Railway boss apologises for Italian train chaos.

text.p: The head of Italy's state railway apologised on Monday to tens of thousands of passengers caught up in a weekend of chaos on the network.
"I apologize to the passengers. Italy's railways are in a backward situation. We have to do much to raise the quality level," president of the state railway Giancarlo Cimoli said.

Travellers were stranded in stations for up to 12 hours after a train derailed in Rome on Saturday and then a crane working to remove it collapsed on Sunday, blocking tracks and effectively slicing the national rail network in two.
Travellers were forced to board crowded buses which ferried them between trains on either side of the divide.
Four passengers suffered minor injuries from the derailment, which happened on one of the busiest weekends of the year for the transport system.
Travel was still disrupted on Monday as engineers struggled to clear the tracks.

Union leaders and members of the centre-right parliamentary opposition heaped criticism on the government and the far-right National Alliance (AN) said it would call a parliamentary vote of no confidence in Transport Minister Claudio Burlando.
"In his declarations there's almost a sense of annoyance about having to explain things to the public," said AN's Publio Fiori, transport minister under the former government of Silvio Berlusconi.
"Otherwise he would have offered to come to parliament to explain what happened and what he intends to do in the future...he's proved himself incapable of carrying out his job."
Burlando, interviewed on Italian national television, described the calls for his resignation as "normal".
Consumer groups demanded one million lire ($550) in compensation for each affected traveller.
Burlando said in a newspaper interview published on Monday that Italy's railway network "faces an infrastructural and technological delay that has perhaps no equal in Europe".
At a news conference later in the day he said the government planned to invest 42 trillion lire ($23 billion) in the rail system over the next three years.
The money will be used to introduce an automatic traffic control system on the nation's main lines and to quadruple the number of tracks connecting north and south within the next five years.
"It is difficult to control the traffic of the year 2000 with structures that go back to 1800s," Burlando said.
He stressed that despite the problems, the train service was safe.
"The number of casualties in rail accidents in Italy is fewer than in the main European countries," he said.
Eight people died last January when a Milan-Rome high speed train derailed near the northern city of Piacenza.
Investigators suspected excess speed caused that accident and newspapers reported that Saturday's derailment might also have been caused by speeding.
